## What does X Tweet Scraper do?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper returns tweets, engagement metrics, public author
profiles & media. It accepts URLs, handles, List IDs, Tweet IDs & search queries
with 50+ filters.

### Use cases

- Feed tweet text, authors, media & metrics into research, enrichment, analytics
  & AI training.
- Track brand sentiment across tweets.
- Monitor competitor posts & industry terms.
- Find prospects in public conversations.
- Collect public datasets for research.
- Find posts with high public engagement.

## Why use X Tweet Scraper?

- **13.6x faster search.** Keyword search ran 13.6x faster than the fastest of 4
  other tweet Actors. Filtered search ran 4.3x faster, & a user timeline about
  3x. The [benchmark](#benchmark) ran on 2026-10-15 & 2026-10-16.
- **Lowest cost per useful tweet.** It cost the least per useful tweet in all 3
  [benchmark](#benchmark) tests.
- **More fields per tweet.** Its median keyword search row had 67 fields. That
  is 1.3x the median of the other Actors in the [benchmark](#benchmark).
- **Every source in 1 run.** Mix Tweet IDs, handles, Lists, searches & URLs in 1
  input. Set `mode` for replies, quotes, threads, mentions, retweeters or
  articles.
- **Find X's top tweets.** `mode: "topTweets"` returns the tweets X ranks
  highest for 1 metric, such as views. Narrow them to a day, week or month & a
  country.
- **Embed code for each tweet.** `mode: "embed"` returns the HTML that shows a
  tweet on your site.
- **No cap on Tweet IDs.** Look up any number of Tweet IDs in 1 run. Rows come
  back in your input order. Your spend limit & timeout still apply.
- **Latest & Top in 1 run.** Set `queryType` to `Latest + Top` for both search
  orders. You pay for each tweet once.

### Complete results

- Large date ranges come back whole & fast.
- Searches return every match, whatever operators you combine.
- Account history comes back complete, old posts included.
- Profile exports keep every post of the author's own threads.
- Profile reads include the pinned post, flagged as pinned.
- Top tweet lists come back reliably.
- Filtered pages come back full until the results run out.
- Each answer holds the fullest data X has for it.

### Accurate rows

- Search results hold every post that matches your query & nothing else.
- Word & phrase matching works in every language & script.
- Language filters work for every language X tags.
- A post is called missing only when it's gone.
- Protected accounts & private Lists get a clear answer, not an empty page.
- Reposts carry the full original text.
- Every ID in a row stays exact.
- Mentions, links, hashtags & highlights line up with the text.
- A count that isn't known is listed in `unknownCounts`, never shown as 0.
- Verified badges match what `x.com` shows.
- Rows hold public data only.
- Quote searches return every real quote & nothing else.
- Reply exports hold only direct replies, in a proven order.
- Newest-first results come back in date order.
- Searches accept queries as you'd type them on X.
- Place searches work with names in 6 languages.
- A search that can't run fails at once & says how to fix it.
- A date means one thing in any common form.
- Searches accept `since_id` & `max_id` bounds.
- Ads & promoted entries never reach your rows.

### Fresh data

- Reads keep working when X ships changes.

### Speed

- One slow page doesn't hold up your run.
- Searches stay fast on busy topics.
- Each next page arrives fast.
- Actors read many handles, posts & queries at once.
- Reads finish the moment their rows arrive.
- Stalled Actor calls recover on their own.

### Fair billing

- Bad input costs nothing & tells you what to fix.
- A post ID listed twice in a batch is billed once.
- Actors charge only for delivered, unique, matching rows.
- A restarted run never charges twice.
- Runs stay within your spend cap & still write their diagnostics.
- Tweet, reply & follower run reports estimate what the run cost.
- Small runs end with a tip that cuts cost.

### Reliability

- A one-off error doesn't fail your run.
- Paging stays consistent from one page to the next.
- Paging never loops forever.
- A deadline returns the rows already found, with diagnostics.
- Actors ride out short Xquik outages.
- Actor runs survive restarts without repeats.
- One bad row doesn't sink a batch.
- Stopped runs keep their rows & their report.
- A run that can't start still explains itself.
- `stopCauses`, `failedSubtargets` & `unavailableTargets` spell out partial
  failures.
- Support can see exactly what a request or run returned.

### Built for agents

- Actors accept input written for other Actors.
- Output is ready for spreadsheets, with flat columns & engagement totals.
- Scraper datasets describe every field.
- Every run says why it ended & whether to retry.

### Rich data

- Posts carry note text, edits, Community Notes, reach labels, reply controls &
  live events.
- Rows carry source apps, media counts & professional account data.
- Media comes with variants, alt text, sizes & availability reasons.
- You see when each account reposted a post.
- Posts & bios can be translated into your language.

### Quality checks

- Every field X shows is served, left out on purpose or proven absent.
- Xquik tests every read live against X.

## What data can X Tweet Scraper extract?

| Field                  | Description                                            |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `id`                   | Tweet ID                                               |
| `text`                 | Full text, including Note Tweets up to 25k chars       |
| `createdAt`            | X native timestamp string                              |
| `likeCount`            | Number of likes                                        |
| `retweetCount`         | Number of retweets                                     |
| `replyCount`           | Number of replies                                      |
| `quoteCount`           | Number of quote tweets                                 |
| `viewCount`            | Number of views                                        |
| `bookmarkCount`        | Number of bookmarks                                    |
| `lang`                 | Tweet language                                         |
| `url`                  | Direct link to tweet                                   |
| `tweetUrl`             | Flat output tweet URL alias                            |
| `twitterUrl`           | Flat output `twitter.com` URL                          |
| `author`               | Author username, bio, website & counts                 |
| `authorUsername`       | Flat output author handle                              |
| `authorFollowers`      | Flat output author follower count                      |
| `authorUrl`            | Flat output author website when available              |
| `authorDescription`    | Flat output author bio text                            |
| `authorCoverPicture`   | Flat output author banner image URL                    |
| `authorPinnedTweetIds` | Flat output author pinned tweet IDs                    |
| `media`                | Attached images, videos, GIFs                          |
| `mediaUrls`            | Flat output media URLs                                 |
| `imageUrls`            | Flat output image URLs                                 |
| `videoUrls`            | Flat output video URLs                                 |
| `entities`             | Hashtags, URLs, mentions, and video timestamps         |
| `displayTextRange`     | X display text range when available                    |
| `contentDisclosure`    | Disclosure metadata when available                     |
| `conversationControl`  | Reply policy and public conversation owner             |
| `reactionContext`      | Public post and user referenced by a reaction          |
| `liveEventContext`     | Live event the post belongs to, such as an election    |
| `subscriberBadge`      | The creator the reply's author subscribes to           |
| `limitedActions`       | Public interaction restrictions and prompts            |
| `isLimitedReply`       | Whether replies are limited                            |
| `isNoteTweet`          | Whether this is a Note Tweet (long-form post)          |
| `isQuoteStatus`        | Whether this tweet quotes another tweet                |
| `isRetweet`            | Whether this row is a retweet, original attached       |
| `isPinned`             | Whether the author pinned this post. Only in flat rows |
| `isReply`              | Whether this tweet is a reply                          |
| `quoted_tweet`         | Quoted tweet object (if quote tweet)                   |
| `conversationId`       | Thread/conversation ID                                 |
| `resultType`           | Row type for rich, engagement & diagnostic rows        |
| `sourceTweetId`        | Source tweet ID for article and engagement modes       |
| `article`              | Structured article data in `mode: "article"`           |
| `translation`          | X's translation in `mode: "translation"`               |
| `embed`                | Embed HTML & link in `mode: "embed"`                   |

Optional tweet metadata includes `authorUnavailable`, `card`,
`cashtagAttachments`, `communityId`, `communityName`, `communityNote`, `edit`,
`exclusiveContent`, `noteTweet` & `postCta`. `isTranslatable`, `place`,
`possiblySensitive` & `viewState` keep other public context. `previousCounts`
keeps pre-edit engagement. `tombstone` keeps visibility notices.
`softIntervention` keeps the label X shows on a tweet whose reach it limits.
`unmentionedUserIds` lists users who left the conversation. See OpenAPI for the
exact fields.

Set `outputVariant: "rich"` for the most data per row. Rich rows add
`hasCommunityNotes`, `quotedTweetPermalink`, `unavailableAuthorId` & media
`sourceUser` at the end. Legacy rows stay unchanged.

Nested `author` objects carry public profile fields. They cover identity,
counts, verification, availability, professional data & profile biographies.

Retweet rows set `isRetweet` to `true`. Their `text` carries the original post
in full. `retweeted_tweet` holds the original post with its author & counts.

Tweet rows also keep `type`, `source`, `inReplyToId`, `inReplyToUserId`,
`inReplyToUsername` & `retweeted_tweet`. Quoted & reposted tweets carry the same
fields at every nesting level.

Media carries availability, geometry, tags & video variants. It also carries the
`watchNowUrl` & `visitSiteUrl` actions.

Rows never include viewer-only state. The Actor removes follow, block, mute,
bookmark, like, repost, edit-permission & similar viewer flags. Raw output drops
them too.

## How do I use X Tweet Scraper to scrape tweet data?

New to Apify?
[Create a free account](https://console.apify.com/sign-up?fpr=xquik) first. The
free plan needs no credit card & gives $5 to spend each month. At $0.00015 per
row, $5 pays for up to 33,000 rows before platform usage. Then come back here &
press Try for free.

Follow these steps in Apify Console.

1. Open a [task example](#task-examples) or the Input tab.
2. Add URLs, handles, Tweet IDs or search terms.
3. Set `maxItems` & any filters you need.
4. Click Start & wait for the run to finish.
5. Export the dataset as JSON, CSV, Excel or HTML.

Each recipe below is a complete input for 1 source. Pick the one that fits your
data.

### Paste URLs

Paste any mix of tweet, profile, search or List URLs.

```json
{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://x.com/jack/status/20" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/nasa" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/search?q=AI%20lang%3Aen" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/i/lists/1748648376080666720" }
  ],
  "maxItems": 500
}
```

Tweet URLs return those tweets, unique & in your input order. Profile URLs
return the account's posts. Search URLs run their query. List URLs return the
List's posts. `maxItems` caps results across all pasted URLs.

### Scrape many handles

Handles return the posts of many accounts in 1 run.

```json
{ "twitterHandles": ["elonmusk", "nasa", "openai"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Each handle returns that account's posts. The Actor removes duplicate rows
before output & billing. You can add usernames with or without `@`. Handles &
profile URLs keep reposts, even with dates or filters. Set
`tweetTypes.excludeRetweets` to drop them.

### Search tweets

Put 1 or more queries in the Search terms field.

```json
{
  "searchTerms": ["from:elonmusk AI", "#bitcoin lang:en"],
  "maxItems": 1000,
  "queryType": "Latest"
}
```

With `mode` set to `tweet` or `tweets` & no Tweet IDs, queries run as Search.
Valid `searchTerms` then never return an empty lookup.

Account backfills with date windows work too, such as
`from:elonmusk since:2026-01-01 until:2026-01-02`. Each term keeps its own
`searchTerm` attribution. `maxItems` caps results across all search terms. The
Actor checks every returned tweet against `since:`, `until:` & Unix-time
windows. Filtered searches keep reading until they find matches or X has no more
results.

A `from:` search term returns what X search returns, so it leaves out reposts.
Add `include:nativeretweets` to keep them, or `filter:nativeretweets` for
reposts only.

### Look up tweets by ID

```json
{ "tweetIds": ["20", "2082577277246972300"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Results keep your input order, drop duplicates & include only the tweets you
asked for. The lookup also accepts `tweetId`, `tweetIDs`, `tweets`, `postIds`,
`lookupPostIds`, `tweetUrls` & `postUrls`.

Each entry is a tweet ID or a tweet URL. The run skips any other entry at no
charge & reads the rest. Its status counts the skipped entries & its log lists
them.

Put all your IDs in 1 run. Each run pays Apify the same start cost. With 1 ID
per run, Apify usage adds about $0.00008 to each tweet. With 188 IDs in 1 run,
it adds about $0.000005. A run of fewer than 5 IDs ends with this tip.

### Engagement, thread & article modes

Set `mode` to pick what the run reads, whatever other fields the input holds.

```json
{ "mode": "replies", "replyTweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Tweet & search modes are `tweet`, `tweets` & `search`. Profile modes are
`profileTweets`, `profileReplies`, `profileMedia`, `profileLikes` &
`profileMentions`. `listTweets` reads List posts, & `article` reads the X
article in a post. Modes for a single post are `replies`, `quotes`, `thread`,
`retweeters`, `favoriters`, `translation` & `embed`.

`profileMentions` returns the posts that mention each handle, newest first.

```json
{ "mode": "profileMentions", "twitterHandles": ["nasa"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

`profileTweets` returns the account's posts, reposts & replies to its own posts.
Rows come in date order. The Actor drops replies to other accounts before
billing. It also drops conversation context from other authors.

For original posts only, exclude the types you do not want.

```json
{
  "mode": "profileTweets",
  "twitterHandles": ["apify"],
  "tweetTypes": { "excludeReplies": true, "excludeRetweets": true },
  "maxItems": 100
}
```

`tweetTypes.excludeReplies`, `excludeRetweets` & `excludeQuotes` work on every
source. Excluded rows never reach the dataset, so you never pay for them. They
never count toward `maxItems` either.

`profileReplies` returns the account's own posts & replies. The Actor excludes
conversation context from other authors. Use `filter:replies` or a `to:` search
for reply-only results.

Search & paginated Tweet modes support `time.since`, `time.until`, Unix
timestamps & `lang`. These include profile Posts, With Replies, Media, Likes,
Lists, replies, quotes & threads. Matching flat date operators work too. The
Actor verifies each row before billing. The lower date bound is inclusive. The
upper bound is exclusive. Date filters exclude rows without usable dates.
Language filters exclude missing or mismatched languages. Filtered rows never
use up your result limit.

The same date for `since` & `until` gives an empty window. Set `until` to the
next day to get 1 full day. List runs with a date window reach older days
quickly. They end once they pass your lower bound. Windows far back in a List
can miss a few replies. Tweet filters do not apply to user lists or direct Tweet
or article lookups.

`time.withinTime` & `within_time` work in the same modes. A value of `7d` keeps
the last 7 days before the run starts reading. A window reaching back before
2006 keeps every post.

`mode: "replies"` is stricter. Every tweet row has `inReplyToId` equal to the
requested tweet ID. Nested conversation replies never count as direct replies.
If X shows fewer replies than it reports, the Actor keeps the rows it found. It
adds 1 `replies-incomplete` record to `diagnostics` when your limit is not
reached. The run stays partial until it reaches your limit or X has no more
replies. `replyCoverage` reports reply counts & coverage details. Set `maxItems`
to the total you want, even above 25,000 for 1 reply target.

Article rows include `resultType: "article"`, `sourceTweetId`, `article` &
optional `author`. Engagement user rows include `resultType: "user"`,
`sourceTweetId` & `engagementMode`.

Retweeters work as a normal public engagement mode. Favoriters are best effort.
X may show likers only on eligible or owner-visible posts. Profile likes are
best effort too, since X shows them only to their owner. If X shows no users or
liked tweets, the run's status says so. Tweet rows can carry bookmark counts. X
does not show which accounts bookmarked a post.

### Translate tweets & get embed HTML

`mode: "translation"` returns X's translation of each tweet. Set `translateTo`
to a language code such as `en`, `es`, `pt-br` or `zh-tw`. It defaults to `en`.

```json
{
  "mode": "translation",
  "tweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"],
  "translateTo": "es"
}
```

Each row has `resultType: "translation"`, `sourceTweetId` & `translation`. That
object holds `language`, `sourceLanguage`, `text` & `entities`.

`mode: "embed"` returns the HTML that embeds each tweet on a website.

```json
{ "mode": "embed", "tweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"], "embedTheme": "dark" }
```

Each row has `resultType: "embed"`, `sourceTweetId` & `embed`. That object holds
`url`, `authorName`, `authorUrl`, `html` & `width`. `embedHideMedia`,
`embedHideThread` & `embedOmitScript` leave media, the parent tweet or the
widget script out.

Both modes take tweet IDs or tweet URLs in `tweetIds`. `startUrls` takes tweet
URLs too. Each tweet gives 1 row at the usual row price. A tweet X does not have
gives no row & no charge.

### Get the top tweets on X

`mode: "topTweets"` returns the tweets X ranks highest by 1 metric.

```json
{
  "mode": "topTweets",
  "topMetric": "views",
  "topWindow": "week",
  "topCountry": "US",
  "maxItems": 100
}
```

`topMetric` is `likes`, `replies`, `quotes`, `bookmarks`, `shares` or `views`.
It defaults to `likes`. `topWindow` is `day`, `week` or `month`, & defaults to
`day`. X lists up to 100 tweets for each choice. Leave `topCountry` empty for
all of X. Set `lang` to keep 1 language. With both set, you get that country's
tweets in that language. Each row has `engagementMode: "topTweets"` & costs 1
result, like any tweet.

### Export flat CSV rows

Keep the default nested JSON fields, or add spreadsheet-friendly columns.

```json
{ "searchTerms": ["from:nasa moon"], "maxItems": 100, "outputPreset": "flat" }
```

Flat output keeps `author` & `media` unchanged. It adds top-level fields such as
`authorUsername`, `authorName`, `authorFollowers`, `tweetUrl`, `twitterUrl`,
`mediaUrls`, `imageUrls` & `videoUrls`.

Every flat tweet row carries `media`. A tweet without media has an empty list.
Each row then has the same keys in a spreadsheet or typed pipeline.

### Choose field names

Legacy field names are the default. Pick a style for rich or raw results.

```json
{
  "searchTerms": ["from:nasa moon"],
  "maxItems": 100,
  "outputVariant": "rich",
  "fieldStyle": "snake_case"
}
```

Use `camelCase` or `snake_case` for top-level & nested result fields. Flat snake
case output includes fields such as `author_username` & `media_urls`. Safe
source snapshots under `raw` keep their original source keys. Conflicting source
names also stay unchanged to prevent data loss.

Legacy diagnostics use `resultType`, `actorVersion` & `replyCoverage`. Rich &
raw output apply `fieldStyle` at every nesting level. For example, snake case
uses `result_type`, `actor_version` & `reply_coverage`. The Overview dataset
view works with either style. Choose the Console view matching the run's
`fieldStyle`. `camelCase fields` expects `camelCase`. `snake_case fields`
expects `snake_case`. Views select columns only. They never rename stored or
exported data.

### Combine advanced filters

Combine user, date, location, media & engagement filters.

```json
{
  "twitterContent": "AI",
  "from": "elonmusk",
  "since": "2026-01-01_00:00:00_UTC",
  "until": "2026-03-01_00:00:00_UTC",
  "lang": "en",
  "filter:media": true,
  "min_faves": 1000,
  "maxItems": 500
}
```

Set `queryType: "Latest + Top"` to run both X search modes in 1 run. The Actor
removes duplicates before billing & fills your limit from either mode. `Top`
sorts by relevance & does not return every match. Set `includeSearchTerms: true`
to attach each matching query as a `searchTerm` field.

When you set `lang`, the Actor verifies each returned tweet's language. It skips
mismatches & keeps reading for matching tweets.

## How much does it cost to scrape tweets?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper costs $0.00015 per delivered row on every Apify plan.
Apify bills your platform usage separately. Xquik applies one charge per
delivered data row. Diagnostics are free in the `diagnostics` output.

For more volume, [pick an Apify plan](https://apify.com/pricing?fpr=xquik) with
more prepaid usage.

- You need no Xquik subscription.
- You pay no separate start or query fee. URLs & single Tweet lookups add no fee
  either.
- Filters & deduplication run before billing. You never pay for filtered or
  duplicate rows.
- No-input & invalid-input runs write 1 actionable record to the free
  `diagnostics` output. So do runs that stop early, skip a target, or whose own
  filters, such as `lang` on a profile read, remove every row.
- A run that reads every target & gets no row back writes no record. Its status
  says why & what to change. Rows your search operators rule out, such as
  `-is:retweet`, write no record either.

A run that hits a problem, or a large run, also writes a `run-report` record.
Its `estimatedChargeUsd` uses the live pay-per-event price from Apify. Runs with
a problem always write `run-report`, including no-input and invalid-input exits.
A small run that goes well skips it & saves Apify usage. Turn on
`alwaysSaveRunRecords` to write it on every run. Run reports separate data rows
in `realRows` from diagnostics in `diagnosticRows`.

To cap what a run can spend, see [Run options](#run-options).

## Benchmark

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper ran 3 benchmarks against 4 other tweet Actors. It was
the fastest in all 3. It also cost the least per useful tweet in all 3.

### Keyword search

Every Actor ran the same search & filters for 1,000 results. Xquik was 13.6x
faster than the fastest other Actor. It also cost the least per useful tweet.
Its median row had 67 fields, 1.3x the median of the others. A useful tweet is a
unique English original post with 10+ likes. It falls in the date range.

## Empty, partial & stopped runs

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper explains empty, partial & stopped runs for free. The run
status says why the run stopped. It also counts charged results & targets read.

### Empty results

Check an empty result before you pay for another run. The `filtering` object in
reports & final diagnostics counts the rows your filters removed. Read
`serverFilteredRows`, `actorFilteredRows` & `pagesWithUnknownServerFiltering`.
You never pay result charges for filtered rows. A run writes 1 diagnostic with
these counts when the Actor's own filters removed rows (`actorFilteredRows`).
Rows your search operators rule out (`serverFilteredRows`), posts outside your
time window & a run that got no row at all write no record. Its status says why
& what to change, such as a broader search.

A run can finish below your limit when X has no more results. It reports
`outcome: "complete"` with `completionReason: "source_exhausted"`. Interrupted
runs keep their partial outcome & retry guidance.

### Partial runs

`failedSubtargets` counts queries & profile targets that stopped after an error.
Delivered rows stay in the dataset & count toward billing. An error never means
the target is missing. These runs use `completionReason: "partial_failure"`.

An interrupted run also writes a free `partial` diagnostic. Results already
delivered stay intact. The diagnostic reports `availableResults`,
`failedTargets`, `retryable` & `nextAction`. A successful Actor exit confirms
delivery. It does not confirm complete extraction.

### Stop causes

The status text names every cause of the stop. A run with a missing account & a
stalled search says both. `stopCauses` lists each cause with its own `message`,
`retryable` & `nextAction`. The causes are `target_not_found`,
`target_suspended`, `target_protected`, `search_unavailable`, `likes_hidden`,
`target_failed`, `pagination_safety_limit`, `reply_reach` & `deadline_reached`.
The run is `retryable` when any cause is.

### Missing & unavailable targets

A missing or protected target is not a failure. X has nothing to read there. The
run reads every other target to the end. It reports `outcome: "complete"`. Its
completion reason comes from the targets it read, such as `source_exhausted`.
`failedSubtargets` leaves those targets out. The status text & a free `complete`
diagnostic count them. A run without other rows writes a `zero-output`
diagnostic instead.

A search X cannot run counts as a failure. X shows "Something went wrong" for
such a search. The run stops it at once without retries. Likes X hides also
count as failures & stop at once. X shows who liked a post only to its author.
It shows an account's liked posts only to that account.

When all failures concern unavailable targets, diagnostics set
`retryable: false`. Check target URLs or usernames & choose available public
accounts. Narrow a search X cannot run or change its filters. Read retweeters,
replies or posts instead of hidden likes. Other failures keep retry guidance for
unfinished targets.

The diagnostic names those targets in `unavailableTargets`. Each entry has the
`target` as you entered it, a `reason` & a `nextAction`. The reason is
`not_found`, `list_not_found`, `suspended`, `protected`, `search_unavailable` or
`likes_hidden`. `list_not_found` marks a list X did not find, which may be
private. A search entry can also have a `fix`, such as the operator to remove.
The list holds up to 100 entries. Remove those targets from your input.

### Safety & time limits

`completionReason: "pagination_safety_limit"` is not a read failure. The run
kept its valid rows. It then ended a target that stopped returning new results.
The run reports incomplete extraction. `failedSubtargets` stays `0`. You pay
only for delivered rows.

The default Apify timeout is `0`, so runs have no time limit. The Actor
continues until it reaches your cap or runs out of eligible data. You can still
set a finite Apify timeout. Then `completionReason: "deadline_reached"` means
that limit is near. The Actor saves rows & the report, then exits cleanly before
the limit. You pay once for each delivered row.

## Output columns

8 inputs shape each row after the run reads it. They run no code & change no
price.

| Field               | What it does                                                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fields`            | Keep only these fields, in the order & spelling you write   |
| `omitFields`        | Drop these fields & keep the rest                           |
| `renameFields`      | Move a field to a column with a new name                    |
| `flatten`           | Turn each nested object into top-level columns              |
| `fillMissingFields` | Fill a kept field a row lacks with `null`. On by default    |
| `joinFields`        | Turn each of these lists into 1 text value                  |
| `joinSeparator`     | Text between joined items. The default is a comma & a space |
| `constantFields`    | Add a column with the same text on every row                |

- Use a dot for a field inside an object, such as `author.id`. Case &
  underscores do not matter.
- Every row keeps its `id`.
- With `fields`, a field a row lacks arrives as `null`. Every row then has the
  same columns.
- A wrong field name stops the run before it reads & charges nothing.
- If names cannot be checked, the run reads on & lists unseen names last.

## FAQ

Answers to common questions, then where to get help.

### Do I need an X API key?

No. You need no X API key, login or credentials.

### What limits a run?

Your item limit & your Apify spend limit stop the run. Apify account & platform
limits still apply.

### How fast is it?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper delivered 150.5 to 172.4 useful tweets per second. That
was in the keyword search [benchmark](#benchmark). Runtime depends on your
input, the result count & X availability.

### Do searches return every matching post?

Yes, until the matches run out or you reach `maxItems`. Results hold only posts
that match your query. You pay for each post once.

### Which search operators work?

X advanced search supports authors, recipients, mentions, dates, engagement,
media & location. See
[Top supported search operators](#top-supported-search-operators) for examples.

### Can I use the Apify API to run this?

Yes. See the [API tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/api) for Python,
JavaScript & cURL examples.

### Can I schedule recurring scrapes?

Yes. Use Apify's built-in
[scheduling](https://docs.apify.com/platform/schedules) to run Xquik's X Tweet
Scraper on a cron.

### Can I get a custom solution?

Yes. Describe what you need in the
[Issues tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/issues). Xquik also offers
a dashboard, a REST API, an MCP server & webhooks. Find Xquik's website on its
[Apify profile](https://apify.com/xquik).

### Is it legal to scrape X data?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper requests public X fields. Results can contain personal
data. Confirm a lawful purpose & follow the privacy rules that apply to you. Ask
qualified counsel when unsure.

### Where do I get help?

Open an issue in the
[Issues tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/issues) with the run ID.

## What does X Tweet Scraper do?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper returns tweets, engagement metrics, public author
profiles & media. It accepts URLs, handles, List IDs, Tweet IDs & search queries
with 50+ filters.

### Use cases

- Feed tweet text, authors, media & metrics into research, enrichment, analytics
  & AI training.
- Track brand sentiment across tweets.
- Monitor competitor posts & industry terms.
- Find prospects in public conversations.
- Collect public datasets for research.
- Find posts with high public engagement.

## Why use X Tweet Scraper?

- **13.6x faster search.** Keyword search ran 13.6x faster than the fastest of 4
  other tweet Actors. Filtered search ran 4.3x faster, & a user timeline about
  3x. The [benchmark](#benchmark) ran on 2026-10-15 & 2026-10-16.
- **Lowest cost per useful tweet.** It cost the least per useful tweet in all 3
  [benchmark](#benchmark) tests.
- **More fields per tweet.** Its median keyword search row had 67 fields. That
  is 1.3x the median of the other Actors in the [benchmark](#benchmark).
- **Every source in 1 run.** Mix Tweet IDs, handles, Lists, searches & URLs in 1
  input. Set `mode` for replies, quotes, threads, mentions, retweeters or
  articles.
- **Find X's top tweets.** `mode: "topTweets"` returns the tweets X ranks
  highest for 1 metric, such as views. Narrow them to a day, week or month & a
  country.
- **Embed code for each tweet.** `mode: "embed"` returns the HTML that shows a

## How do I use X Tweet Scraper to scrape tweet data?

New to Apify?
[Create a free account](https://console.apify.com/sign-up?fpr=xquik) first. The
free plan needs no credit card & gives $5 to spend each month. At $0.00015 per
row, $5 pays for up to 33,000 rows before platform usage. Then come back here &
press Try for free.

Follow these steps in Apify Console.

1. Open a [task example](#task-examples) or the Input tab.
2. Add URLs, handles, Tweet IDs or search terms.
3. Set `maxItems` & any filters you need.
4. Click Start & wait for the run to finish.
5. Export the dataset as JSON, CSV, Excel or HTML.

Each recipe below is a complete input for 1 source. Pick the one that fits your
data.

### Paste URLs

Paste any mix of tweet, profile, search or List URLs.

```json
{
  "startUrls": [
    { "url": "https://x.com/jack/status/20" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/nasa" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/search?q=AI%20lang%3Aen" },
    { "url": "https://x.com/i/lists/1748648376080666720" }
  ],
  "maxItems": 500
}
```

Tweet URLs return those tweets, unique & in your input order. Profile URLs
return the account's posts. Search URLs run their query. List URLs return the
List's posts. `maxItems` caps results across all pasted URLs.

### Scrape many handles

Handles return the posts of many accounts in 1 run.

```json
{ "twitterHandles": ["elonmusk", "nasa", "openai"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Each handle returns that account's posts. The Actor removes duplicate rows
before output & billing. You can add usernames with or without `@`. Handles &
profile URLs keep reposts, even with dates or filters. Set
`tweetTypes.excludeRetweets` to drop them.

### Search tweets

Put 1 or more queries in the Search terms field.

```json
{
  "searchTerms": ["from:elonmusk AI", "#bitcoin lang:en"],
  "maxItems": 1000,
  "queryType": "Latest"
}
```

With `mode` set to `tweet` or `tweets` & no Tweet IDs, queries run as Search.
Valid `searchTerms` then never return an empty lookup.

Account backfills with date windows work too, such as
`from:elonmusk since:2026-01-01 until:2026-01-02`. Each term keeps its own
`searchTerm` attribution. `maxItems` caps results across all search terms. The
Actor checks every returned tweet against `since:`, `until:` & Unix-time
windows. Filtered searches keep reading until they find matches or X has no more
results.

A `from:` search term returns what X search returns, so it leaves out reposts.
Add `include:nativeretweets` to keep them, or `filter:nativeretweets` for
reposts only.

### Look up tweets by ID

```json
{ "tweetIds": ["20", "2082577277246972300"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Results keep your input order, drop duplicates & include only the tweets you
asked for. The lookup also accepts `tweetId`, `tweetIDs`, `tweets`, `postIds`,
`lookupPostIds`, `tweetUrls` & `postUrls`.

Each entry is a tweet ID or a tweet URL. The run skips any other entry at no
charge & reads the rest. Its status counts the skipped entries & its log lists
them.

Put all your IDs in 1 run. Each run pays Apify the same start cost. With 1 ID
per run, Apify usage adds about $0.00008 to each tweet. With 188 IDs in 1 run,
it adds about $0.000005. A run of fewer than 5 IDs ends with this tip.

### Engagement, thread & article modes

Set `mode` to pick what the run reads, whatever other fields the input holds.

```json
{ "mode": "replies", "replyTweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

Tweet & search modes are `tweet`, `tweets` & `search`. Profile modes are
`profileTweets`, `profileReplies`, `profileMedia`, `profileLikes` &
`profileMentions`. `listTweets` reads List posts, & `article` reads the X
article in a post. Modes for a single post are `replies`, `quotes`, `thread`,
`retweeters`, `favoriters`, `translation` & `embed`.

`profileMentions` returns the posts that mention each handle, newest first.

```json
{ "mode": "profileMentions", "twitterHandles": ["nasa"], "maxItems": 100 }
```

`profileTweets` returns the account's posts, reposts & replies to its own posts.
Rows come in date order. The Actor drops replies to other accounts before
billing. It also drops conversation context from other authors.

For original posts only, exclude the types you do not want.

```json
{
  "mode": "profileTweets",
  "twitterHandles": ["apify"],
  "tweetTypes": { "excludeReplies": true, "excludeRetweets": true },
  "maxItems": 100
}
```

`tweetTypes.excludeReplies`, `excludeRetweets` & `excludeQuotes` work on every
source. Excluded rows never reach the dataset, so you never pay for them. They
never count toward `maxItems` either.

`profileReplies` returns the account's own posts & replies. The Actor excludes
conversation context from other authors. Use `filter:replies` or a `to:` search
for reply-only results.

Search & paginated Tweet modes support `time.since`, `time.until`, Unix
timestamps & `lang`. These include profile Posts, With Replies, Media, Likes,
Lists, replies, quotes & threads. Matching flat date operators work too. The
Actor verifies each row before billing. The lower date bound is inclusive. The
upper bound is exclusive. Date filters exclude rows without usable dates.
Language filters exclude missing or mismatched languages. Filtered rows never
use up your result limit.

The same date for `since` & `until` gives an empty window. Set `until` to the
next day to get 1 full day. List runs with a date window reach older days
quickly. They end once they pass your lower bound. Windows far back in a List
can miss a few replies. Tweet filters do not apply to user lists or direct Tweet
or article lookups.

`time.withinTime` & `within_time` work in the same modes. A value of `7d` keeps
the last 7 days before the run starts reading. A window reaching back before
2006 keeps every post.

`mode: "replies"` is stricter. Every tweet row has `inReplyToId` equal to the
requested tweet ID. Nested conversation replies never count as direct replies.
If X shows fewer replies than it reports, the Actor keeps the rows it found. It
adds 1 `replies-incomplete` record to `diagnostics` when your limit is not
reached. The run stays partial until it reaches your limit or X has no more
replies. `replyCoverage` reports reply counts & coverage details. Set `maxItems`
to the total you want, even above 25,000 for 1 reply target.

Article rows include `resultType: "article"`, `sourceTweetId`, `article` &
optional `author`. Engagement user rows include `resultType: "user"`,
`sourceTweetId` & `engagementMode`.

Retweeters work as a normal public engagement mode. Favoriters are best effort.
X may show likers only on eligible or owner-visible posts. Profile likes are
best effort too, since X shows them only to their owner. If X shows no users or
liked tweets, the run's status says so. Tweet rows can carry bookmark counts. X
does not show which accounts bookmarked a post.

### Translate tweets & get embed HTML

`mode: "translation"` returns X's translation of each tweet. Set `translateTo`
to a language code such as `en`, `es`, `pt-br` or `zh-tw`. It defaults to `en`.

```json
{
  "mode": "translation",
  "tweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"],
  "translateTo": "es"
}
```

Each row has `resultType: "translation"`, `sourceTweetId` & `translation`. That
object holds `language`, `sourceLanguage`, `text` & `entities`.

`mode: "embed"` returns the HTML that embeds each tweet on a website.

```json
{ "mode": "embed", "tweetIds": ["2082577277246972300"], "embedTheme": "dark" }
```

Each row has `resultType: "embed"`, `sourceTweetId` & `embed`. That object holds
`url`, `authorName`, `authorUrl`, `html` & `width`. `embedHideMedia`,
`embedHideThread` & `embedOmitScript` leave media, the parent tweet or the
widget script out.

Both modes take tweet IDs or tweet URLs in `tweetIds`. `startUrls` takes tweet
URLs too. Each tweet gives 1 row at the usual row price. A tweet X does not have
gives no row & no charge.

### Get the top tweets on X

`mode: "topTweets"` returns the tweets X ranks highest by 1 metric.

```json
{
  "mode": "topTweets",
  "topMetric": "views",
  "topWindow": "week",
  "topCountry": "US",
  "maxItems": 100
}
```

`topMetric` is `likes`, `replies`, `quotes`, `bookmarks`, `shares` or `views`.
It defaults to `likes`. `topWindow` is `day`, `week` or `month`, & defaults to
`day`. X lists up to 100 tweets for each choice. Leave `topCountry` empty for
all of X. Set `lang` to keep 1 language. With both set, you get that country's
tweets in that language. Each row has `engagementMode: "topTweets"` & costs 1
result, like any tweet.

### Export flat CSV rows

Keep the default nested JSON fields, or add spreadsheet-friendly columns.

```json
{ "searchTerms": ["from:nasa moon"], "maxItems": 100, "outputPreset": "flat" }
```

Flat output keeps `author` & `media` unchanged. It adds top-level fields such as
`authorUsername`, `authorName`, `authorFollowers`, `tweetUrl`, `twitterUrl`,
`mediaUrls`, `imageUrls` & `videoUrls`.

Every flat tweet row carries `media`. A tweet without media has an empty list.
Each row then has the same keys in a spreadsheet or typed pipeline.

### Choose field names

Legacy field names are the default. Pick a style for rich or raw results.

```json
{
  "searchTerms": ["from:nasa moon"],
  "maxItems": 100,
  "outputVariant": "rich",
  "fieldStyle": "snake_case"
}
```

Use `camelCase` or `snake_case` for top-level & nested result fields. Flat snake
case output includes fields such as `author_username` & `media_urls`. Safe
source snapshots under `raw` keep their original source keys. Conflicting source
names also stay unchanged to prevent data loss.

Legacy diagnostics use `resultType`, `actorVersion` & `replyCoverage`. Rich &
raw output apply `fieldStyle` at every nesting level. For example, snake case
uses `result_type`, `actor_version` & `reply_coverage`. The Overview dataset
view works with either style. Choose the Console view matching the run's
`fieldStyle`. `camelCase fields` expects `camelCase`. `snake_case fields`
expects `snake_case`. Views select columns only. They never rename stored or
exported data.

### Combine advanced filters

Combine user, date, location, media & engagement filters.

```json
{
  "twitterContent": "AI",
  "from": "elonmusk",
  "since": "2026-01-01_00:00:00_UTC",
  "until": "2026-03-01_00:00:00_UTC",
  "lang": "en",
  "filter:media": true,
  "min_faves": 1000,
  "maxItems": 500
}
```

Set `queryType: "Latest + Top"` to run both X search modes in 1 run. The Actor
removes duplicates before billing & fills your limit from either mode. `Top`
sorts by relevance & does not return every match. Set `includeSearchTerms: true`
to attach each matching query as a `searchTerm` field.

When you set `lang`, the Actor verifies each returned tweet's language. It skips
mismatches & keeps reading for matching tweets.

## Empty, partial & stopped runs

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper explains empty, partial & stopped runs for free. The run
status says why the run stopped. It also counts charged results & targets read.

### Empty results

Check an empty result before you pay for another run. The `filtering` object in
reports & final diagnostics counts the rows your filters removed. Read
`serverFilteredRows`, `actorFilteredRows` & `pagesWithUnknownServerFiltering`.
You never pay result charges for filtered rows. A run writes 1 diagnostic with
these counts when the Actor's own filters removed rows (`actorFilteredRows`).
Rows your search operators rule out (`serverFilteredRows`), posts outside your
time window & a run that got no row at all write no record. Its status says why
& what to change, such as a broader search.

A run can finish below your limit when X has no more results. It reports
`outcome: "complete"` with `completionReason: "source_exhausted"`. Interrupted
runs keep their partial outcome & retry guidance.

### Partial runs

`failedSubtargets` counts queries & profile targets that stopped after an error.
Delivered rows stay in the dataset & count toward billing. An error never means
the target is missing. These runs use `completionReason: "partial_failure"`.

An interrupted run also writes a free `partial` diagnostic. Results already
delivered stay intact. The diagnostic reports `availableResults`,
`failedTargets`, `retryable` & `nextAction`. A successful Actor exit confirms
delivery. It does not confirm complete extraction.

### Stop causes

The status text names every cause of the stop. A run with a missing account & a
stalled search says both. `stopCauses` lists each cause with its own `message`,
`retryable` & `nextAction`. The causes are `target_not_found`,
`target_suspended`, `target_protected`, `search_unavailable`, `likes_hidden`,
`target_failed`, `pagination_safety_limit`, `reply_reach` & `deadline_reached`.
The run is `retryable` when any cause is.

### Missing & unavailable targets

A missing or protected target is not a failure. X has nothing to read there. The
run reads every other target to the end. It reports `outcome: "complete"`. Its
completion reason comes from the targets it read, such as `source_exhausted`.
`failedSubtargets` leaves those targets out. The status text & a free `complete`
diagnostic count them. A run without other rows writes a `zero-output`
diagnostic instead.

A search X cannot run counts as a failure. X shows "Something went wrong" for
such a search. The run stops it at once without retries. Likes X hides also
count as failures & stop at once. X shows who liked a post only to its author.
It shows an account's liked posts only to that account.

When all failures concern unavailable targets, diagnostics set
`retryable: false`. Check target URLs or usernames & choose available public
accounts. Narrow a search X cannot run or change its filters. Read retweeters,
replies or posts instead of hidden likes. Other failures keep retry guidance for
unfinished targets.

The diagnostic names those targets in `unavailableTargets`. Each entry has the
`target` as you entered it, a `reason` & a `nextAction`. The reason is
`not_found`, `list_not_found`, `suspended`, `protected`, `search_unavailable` or
`likes_hidden`. `list_not_found` marks a list X did not find, which may be
private. A search entry can also have a `fix`, such as the operator to remove.
The list holds up to 100 entries. Remove those targets from your input.

### Safety & time limits

`completionReason: "pagination_safety_limit"` is not a read failure. The run
kept its valid rows. It then ended a target that stopped returning new results.
The run reports incomplete extraction. `failedSubtargets` stays `0`. You pay
only for delivered rows.

The default Apify timeout is `0`, so runs have no time limit. The Actor
continues until it reaches your cap or runs out of eligible data. You can still
set a finite Apify timeout. Then `completionReason: "deadline_reached"` means
that limit is near. The Actor saves rows & the report, then exits cleanly before
the limit. You pay once for each delivered row.

## Output columns

8 inputs shape each row after the run reads it. They run no code & change no
price.

| Field               | What it does                                                |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
| `fields`            | Keep only these fields, in the order & spelling you write   |
| `omitFields`        | Drop these fields & keep the rest                           |
| `renameFields`      | Move a field to a column with a new name                    |
| `flatten`           | Turn each nested object into top-level columns              |
| `fillMissingFields` | Fill a kept field a row lacks with `null`. On by default    |
| `joinFields`        | Turn each of these lists into 1 text value                  |
| `joinSeparator`     | Text between joined items. The default is a comma & a space |
| `constantFields`    | Add a column with the same text on every row                |

- Use a dot for a field inside an object, such as `author.id`. Case &
  underscores do not matter.
- Every row keeps its `id`.
- With `fields`, a field a row lacks arrives as `null`. Every row then has the
  same columns.
- A wrong field name stops the run before it reads & charges nothing.
- If names cannot be checked, the run reads on & lists unseen names last.
- The run ignores a map function or jq filter written for another Actor.

Name a computed column in `fields` or `renameFields` to add it.

| Column              | Formula                                                                            |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `totalEngagement`   | `likeCount` + `replyCount` + `retweetCount` + `quoteCount`. A missing count adds 0 |
| `engagementRate`    | `totalEngagement` × 100 ÷ the author's `followers`, to 4 decimals                  |
| `engagementPerView` | `totalEngagement` × 100 ÷ `viewCount`, to 4 decimals                               |

`totalEngagement` is `null` for a row without those counts. A rate is `null`
when its divisor is missing or 0.

## FAQ

Answers to common questions, then where to get help.

### Do I need an X API key?

No. You need no X API key, login or credentials.

### What limits a run?

Your item limit & your Apify spend limit stop the run. Apify account & platform
limits still apply.

### How fast is it?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper delivered 150.5 to 172.4 useful tweets per second. That
was in the keyword search [benchmark](#benchmark). Runtime depends on your
input, the result count & X availability.

### Do searches return every matching post?

Yes, until the matches run out or you reach `maxItems`. Results hold only posts
that match your query. You pay for each post once.

### Which search operators work?

X advanced search supports authors, recipients, mentions, dates, engagement,
media & location. See
[Top supported search operators](#top-supported-search-operators) for examples.

### Can I use the Apify API to run this?

Yes. See the [API tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/api) for Python,
JavaScript & cURL examples.

### Can I schedule recurring scrapes?

Yes. Use Apify's built-in
[scheduling](https://docs.apify.com/platform/schedules) to run Xquik's X Tweet
Scraper on a cron.

### Can I get a custom solution?

Yes. Describe what you need in the
[Issues tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/issues). Xquik also offers
a dashboard, a REST API, an MCP server & webhooks. Find Xquik's website on its
[Apify profile](https://apify.com/xquik).

### Is it legal to scrape X data?

Xquik's X Tweet Scraper requests public X fields. Results can contain personal
data. Confirm a lawful purpose & follow the privacy rules that apply to you. Ask
qualified counsel when unsure.

### Where do I get help?

Open an issue in the
[Issues tab](https://apify.com/xquik/x-tweet-scraper/issues) with the run ID.

input.title: X Tweet Scraper input
input.description: Scrape posts from URLs, profiles, searches, Lists, threads, replies, quote Tweets, articles, and media. Look up Tweets in batches, translate them, get their embed HTML, or collect retweeters and likers. Profile likes and likers are best effort.

startUrls.title: Start URLs
startUrls.description: Add Tweet, profile, search, or List URLs as strings or {"url":"..."} objects. Profile URLs may use /with_replies, /media, or best-effort /likes. For example, ["https://x.com/elonmusk", "https://x.com/search?q=AI"].

twitterContent.title: Search query
twitterContent.description: Search query using X advanced search syntax. Supports keywords, hashtags, exact phrases, boolean operators, and date or Unix time windows. Every returned tweet falls inside your dates. For example, web scraping OR #datascience.

searchTerms.title: Search terms
searchTerms.description: Run multiple searches in one Actor run. Max Items applies across the run. Every result matches the date and Unix time operators in its term. For example, from:elonmusk AI, #bitcoin lang:en.
prefill: (AI agent OR coding agent OR agentic AI) (launch OR release OR benchmark OR open source) lang:en -filter:nativeretweets

twitterHandles.title: X handles
twitterHandles.description: X usernames whose posts to collect. Profile Tweets returns posts, reposts & the author's replies to their own posts. Add Exclude replies under Tweet type filters for original posts only. Profile With Replies keeps target-authored posts and replies. Add usernames with or without @. For example, elonmusk, @nasa.

profileUrls.title: Profile URLs
profileUrls.description: Alias for Start URLs. Add profile URL strings or {"url":"..."} objects.

tweetIds.title: Tweet IDs
tweetIds.description: Tweet IDs or tweet URLs to look up directly. The run skips any other entry at no charge. Other sources in the same input run too, and Max Items applies across the run. There is no fixed ID count cap. For example, 20.

listIds.title: List IDs
listIds.description: X List IDs whose posts to collect. It is usually much faster than List URLs or the List ID filter below. For example, 1748648376080666720.

mode.title: Mode
mode.description: Auto picks a mode from your input. Choose a mode to force one. Profile Tweets returns posts, reposts & the author's replies to their own posts. Profile With Replies keeps target-authored posts and replies. Profile Mentions returns posts that mention each handle, newest first. Translation returns X's translation of each Tweet. Embed HTML returns the markup that embeds each Tweet. Top tweets returns the tweets X ranks highest by 1 metric over a day, week or month. Tweet modes without Tweet IDs use Search when query input is present.

maxItems.title: Max items
maxItems.description: Optional result cap across the whole run. Leave empty to use your Apify max total charge as the result limit when set. Without a spend cap, Xquik uses its built-in default. The Apify pricing box shows the current per-result price before the run starts. Diagnostic rows count toward this cap. The form starts at 1,000. A run can return 100,000 rows & more, so raise it for a full export.

errorMessage.type: Max Items must be a whole number.
errorMessage.minimum: Max Items must be at least 1.

maxItemsPerTarget.title: Max items per target
maxItemsPerTarget.description: Optional cap for each target in multi-target modes.

errorMessage.type: Max Items Per Target must be a whole number.
errorMessage.minimum: Max Items Per Target must be at least 1.

queryType.title: Sort by
queryType.description: Latest returns newest first. Top is ranked by relevance and is not exhaustive. Latest + Top returns both without duplicates and fills your limit from either. Account timelines ignore this setting.

errorMessage.enum: Choose Latest, Top, or Latest + Top.

content.title: Structured content filters
content.description: Build content filters without writing X search syntax.

allWords.title: All words
allWords.description: Words that should appear in the tweet text.

anyWords.title: Any words
anyWords.description: Any of these words may appear.

users.title: Structured user filters
users.description: Optional structured author, reply, mention, and list filters.

from.title: From user
from.description: Only include tweets from this username.

to.title: To user
to.description: Only include replies to this username.

mention.title: Mention user
mention.description: Only include tweets mentioning this username.

list.title: List ID
list.description: Only include tweets from members of this list.

time.title: Date range
time.description: Keep posts from a date window. Use dates, Unix times, a recent window such as 2d, or post IDs.

since.title: Since date
since.description: Only include tweets on or after this date. Write YYYY-MM-DD, such as 2026-01-31. 31/01/2026 & 01/31/2026 also work. A date that fits both orders reads month first, so 04/01/2026 is 1 April. The Actor verifies each result.

until.title: Until date
until.description: Only include tweets before this date. It takes the same date forms as Since date. The Actor verifies each result.

sinceTime.title: Since Unix time
sinceTime.description: Only include tweets on or after this time. Write Unix seconds, such as 1767225600. An ISO 8601 time such as 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z works too, & so do the date forms of Since date. The Actor verifies each result.

untilTime.title: Until Unix time
untilTime.description: Only include tweets before this time. It takes the same forms as Since Unix time. The Actor verifies each result.

sinceId.title: Since Tweet ID
sinceId.description: Only include tweets newer than this ID.

maxId.title: Max Tweet ID
maxId.description: Only include tweets older than this ID.

withinTime.title: Within time
withinTime.description: Only include tweets from the last time window.

maxRetweets.title: Maximum retweets
maxRetweets.description: Only include tweets with at most this many retweets.

maxLikes.title: Maximum likes
maxLikes.description: Only include tweets with at most this many likes.

maxReplies.title: Maximum replies
maxReplies.description: Only include tweets with at most this many replies.

lang.title: Language
lang.description: Filter tweets by language using a 2-letter ISO 639-1 code. Every returned tweet matches this language.

tweetTypes.title: Structured Tweet type filters
tweetTypes.description: Optional tweet type filters. Include only one type, or exclude replies, reposts or quote tweets.

news.title: News
news.description: X no longer supports this filter. A search with it ends with a free diagnostic.

excludeReplies.title: Exclude replies
excludeReplies.description: Drop replies, including the author's replies to their own posts. Use it with a profile to get original posts only.

near.title: Near place
near.description: Keep tweets for a place, such as United States or San Francisco.

within.title: Within radius
within.description: X search no longer supports this filter. A run with it stops at once & says so. Use Near place alone.

geocode.title: Geocode
geocode.description: X search no longer supports this filter. A run with it stops at once & says so.

name.title: Card name
name.description: Keeps only tweets with this card type, such as poll2choice_text_only. The Actor checks each tweet.

url.title: URL
url.description: Only include tweets containing this URL or domain.

source.title: Source app
source.description: X search no longer supports this filter. A run with it stops at once & says so.

excludeSource.title: Exclude source app
excludeSource.description: X search no longer supports this filter. A run with it stops at once & says so.

conversation_id.title: Conversation ID
conversation_id.description: Only include tweets belonging to this conversation thread. Use the first tweet's ID in the thread.

conversationIds.title: Conversation IDs
conversationIds.description: Alias for one or more conversation_id searches.

quoted_tweet_id.title: Quoted Tweet ID
quoted_tweet_id.description: Only include tweets that quote this specific tweet ID.

quoted_user_id.title: Quoted user ID
quoted_user_id.description: Only include tweets that quote any tweet from this user ID.

filter:has_engagement.title: Has engagement
filter:has_engagement.description: Only include tweets with at least one like, retweet, or reply.

include:nativeretweets.title: Include native retweets
include:nativeretweets.description: Include native retweets in results (excluded by default).

filter:twimg.title: Has twimg
filter:twimg.description: Only include tweets containing twimg.com images.

filter:native_video.title: Has native video
filter:native_video.description: Only include tweets with natively uploaded video.

filter:vine.title: Has vine
filter:vine.description: X no longer supports this filter. A search with it ends with a free diagnostic.

filter:consumer_video.title: Has consumer video
filter:consumer_video.description: X no longer supports this filter. A search with it ends with a free diagnostic.

filter:pro_video.title: Has pro video
filter:pro_video.description: X no longer supports this filter. A search with it ends with a free diagnostic.

filter:spaces.title: Has spaces

outputVariant.title: Output variant
outputVariant.description: Legacy preserves compatibility. Rich adds normalized public fields. Raw snapshot also adds a sanitized source snapshot. Compact and Full are Legacy aliases.

errorMessage.enum: Choose Legacy, Rich, Raw snapshot, or a Legacy alias.

fieldStyle.title: Field style
fieldStyle.description: Controls top-level and nested field names for rich and raw results, including reply diagnostics. Use camelCase for JavaScript and TypeScript. respectProfileSubpages.title: Respect profile subpages
respectProfileSubpages.description: Honor profile subpage paths such as /with_replies, /media, and /likes in profile URLs. /with_replies returns target-authored posts and replies. The Actor excludes conversation context from other authors.

quoteTweetIds.title: Quote Tweet IDs

topWindow.title: Top tweets window

embedHideThread.title: Embed without the parent Tweet

embedOmitScript.title: Embed without the widget script

from.title: From user

to.title: To user
to.description: Only include tweets that are replies to this username (without @). For example, OpenAI.

@.title: Mentioned user (@)

since.title: Since date
since.description: Keep posts from this date onward. Write YYYY-MM-DD, or YYYY-MM-DD_HH:MM:SS_UTC for a time of day. 31/01/2026 & 01/31/2026 also work. A date that fits both orders reads month first, so 04/01/2026 is 1 April. The Actor checks each post's date. For example, 2026-01-01_00:00:00_UTC.

until.title: Until date
until.description: Keep posts from before this date. It takes the same date forms as Since date. The Actor checks each post's date. For example, 2026-04-01_00:00:00_UTC.

since_time.title: Since time
since_time.description: Keep posts from this Unix time onward, in seconds. An ISO 8601 time such as 2024-01-01T00:00:00Z works too. The Actor checks each post's time. For example, 1704067200.

until_time.title: Until time
until_time.description: Keep posts from before this Unix time, in seconds. An ISO 8601 time such as 2024-04-01T00:00:00Z works too. The Actor checks each post's time. For example, 1711929600.

within_time.title: Within time
within_time.description: Only include tweets from the last N days, hours, minutes or seconds. Put d, h, m or s after the number. For example, 12h.

since_id.title: Since ID

max_id.title: Max ID

includeUnavailableFields.description: Deprecated compatibility input. Safe availability fields are already included when X provides them.

includeOriginalTweet.title: Include original Tweet
includeOriginalTweet.description: Deprecated compatibility input. Look up source tweets separately with Tweet IDs.

fields.title: Fields to keep
fields.description: Keep only these fields in each row. Pick names or type your own. Use a dot for a field inside an object, such as author.id. Columns arrive in the order & spelling you write. Every row keeps its id. Leave empty for every field. The price per row stays the same. A wrong name stops the run before it reads, at no charge. If names cannot be checked, the run reads on & lists unseen names last.
fields.sectionDescription: Choose, rename, flatten & join the fields of each row. These options run no code & change no price.

omitFields.title: Fields to drop
omitFields.description: Drop these fields & keep the rest. Every row keeps its id.

renameFields.title: Rename fields
renameFields.description: Give a field a new column name. The key is the field. The value is the new name. A renamed field becomes a top-level column.

flatten.title: Flat columns
flatten.description: Turn each nested object into top-level columns, such as authorId. Lists stay lists. Use it for CSV & spreadsheets.

fillMissingFields.title: Fill missing fields with null
fillMissingFields.description: With Fields to keep, a field a row lacks arrives as null. Every row then has the same columns. Turn it off to leave such fields out.

joinFields.title: Lists to join
joinFields.description: Turn each of these lists into 1 text value. Use it for CSV cells.

joinSeparator.title: Join separator
joinSeparator.description: Text between the items of a joined list.

constantFields.title: Constant columns
constantFields.description: Add a column with the same text on every row. The key is the column name, such as campaign. The value is its text.

output.title: X Tweet Scraper output
output.description: Links to the default dataset and run report for a completed X Tweet Scraper run.

tweets.title: Tweets
tweets.description: Unique dataset rows returned by the Actor. Each tweet appears once across searches and terms. Rows match your search dates and Unix times. A Tweet ID lookup returns each requested ID once. Profile Tweets returns posts, reposts & the author's replies to their own posts. Profile With Replies keeps target-authored posts and replies. Profile rows leave out other authors' conversation context. Rows can contain tweets, articles, translations, embeds, or users.

diagnostics.title: Diagnostics
diagnostics.description: Free actionable diagnostics, written only when something needs attention. They cover partial, invalid, aborted & recovered runs. A run that skipped missing or protected accounts writes 1 too. So does an empty run whose own filters removed rows. Rows the search operators rule out write none. A run that read every target & got no row back writes none. A partial diagnostic lists each stop cause in stopCauses. Real results remain in the dataset.

runReport.title: Run report
runReport.description: Run summary with data and diagnostic totals, duration, outcome, completion reason, and anomalies. pagination_safety_limit means the read stopped finding new results. The Actor kept the valid rows. A run writes it when it hits a problem, is large or has Always save run records on. Small runs that go well skip it & state the outcome in their status.
